newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Kohl shruggs off doubters, says EMU a must.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Kohl shruggs off doubters, says EMU a must.

text.p: Shrugging off mounting scepticism over whether Germany can qualify for European monetary union, Chancellor Helmut Kohl said on Wednesday the single currency plan must go forward and that Germany will be a founding member.
Kohl told the lower house of parliament that the single European currency was crucial to European peace and prosperity and that to delay EMU now would risk the euro never getting off the ground.

"A delay would have an enormous impact on financial markets and the export prospects of the German economy," Kohl said. "A common currency is a condition for peace and freedom and the building of a European home."

The chancellor tried to appear confident about Germany's ability to qualify for EMU, despite an embarassing climb-down by Finance Minister Theo Waigel following an open confrontation with the Bundesbank.

As he has said countless times in the past, Kohl insisted terms for joining EMU as stipulated in the Maastricht Treaty must not be watered down and pledged that Germany would solve budget problems that analysts say make its qualification for EMU questionable.

Kohl said he expected a good result to come from talks between the Bundesbank and Waigel over the government's plans to revalue the central bank's official reserves -- a scheme that has been firmly rejected by Bundesbank council members as an attack on their independence.

Under an preliminary, oral agreement beween Waigel and Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer Tuesday, reserves, including gold, are to be revalued this year, but profits not transfered to Bonn unitl 1998.
Waigel had originally hoped to transfer the profits this year, netting the government a windfall that could be used to reduce debt and help Germany qualify for EMU.
Although it appears that Bonn will not get its hands on Bundesbank profits in time to help it qualify for EMU, Kohl pledged Bonn would get its financial house in order.
"I am totally certain that we can master our (budget) problems," he said.

Germany must reduce its budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product by the end of 1997 to qualify for EMU. That ratio stood at 3.8 percent last year and many economists doubt Bonn can reach the three percent goal this year.
Kohl also stood firmly by his finance minister who has been attacked by opposition politicians for challenging the highly-respected Bundesbank.
"You know he will stay in office," Kohl told opposition deputies in German parliament shortly before the governing coalition parties mustered a majority to reject an opposition motion to sack Waigel.
Waigel had earlier said he and Tietmeyer would do their best to have revaluation profits transfered to Bonn's budget from 1998.
